explanation: Partition R into the low-weight indices w(i) <= c and the high-weight indices w(i) > c. Their cardinalities add to #R, so the assumed bound for the low part gives #(high) >= (1-eta)#R. Multiplication by the nonnegative cutoff c preserves this inequality. Every high index contributes at least c, and all remaining weights are nonnegative, hence c#(high) <= sum_{i in R} w(i). Combining these inequalities gives the claimed lower bound. The original same-file theorem cutoff_mul_high_count_le_sum is retained with its complete proof as an inline helper.
natural_language_statement: Let $R$ be a finite set of indices, let $w$ assign a real weight to each index, and let $c,\eta\in\mathbb R$. Assume $c\ge 0$ and $w(i)\ge 0$ for every $i\in R$. If the number of indices with weight at most $c$ satisfies $$\#\{i\in R:w(i)\le c\}\le\eta\,\#R,$$ then $$c(1-\eta)\,\#R\le\sum_{i\in R}w(i).$$ No separate restriction on $\eta$ is required. This finite counting estimate turns an upper bound on the number of low-weight indices into a lower bound for the total weight.
theorem_title: A lower bound for a nonnegative weighted sum from a low-weight count
